claim: CodeVetter can observe bounded first-callback delay for closed async resource categories inside one capture-scoped owned Node request while refusing to equate async context or temporal overlap with awaited critical-path work.

observed: An awaited 20 ms timer was retained under its exact captured request without application source changes.
A timer created by the same handler but completed after the response was excluded.
Filesystem events normalize to a closed category without filename, resource object, callback arguments, or raw async identity.
Overlapping delay intervals are unioned rather than summed, public resources are bounded to eight per request, and stream truncation makes the inventory incomplete.

real_product.verdict: The request context contained a 498.46 ms timer callback delay, but no contained creation call site was resolved. CodeVetter retained the observation and refused to authorize an edit because request-context propagation does not prove that the response awaited the timer or that it was on the critical path.

claim_boundaries: AsyncLocalStorage context proves propagation from a captured request, not an awaited relationship or critical-path causation.
First-callback delay is not exclusive wait time and may overlap CPU, I/O, or other callbacks.
The public inventory is diagnostic and bounded; incomplete evidence cannot support absence claims.
Resource values, raw async identities, filenames, hosts, addresses, requested delay values, and callback arguments are not retained.
A config-disabled Next development runtime, failed product assertion, system Chrome, and one local machine do not establish production frequency or impact.
A source edit still requires a contained candidate plus correctness-passing paired end-to-end improvement.
